claims.text: Enhanced atomic mixing entropy governs the premelting and melting behavior of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Enhanced mixing entropy suppresses local elemental segregation in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Enhanced mixing entropy suppresses surface premelting.
Near-equimolar mixing of multiple elements increases mixing entropy.
For an equimolar multielement vapor, the partial pressure of each constituent is reduced according to P_i = P_total/N.
The reduced-partial-pressure relation applicable during vapor-phase synthesis also operates during thermal activation of already-formed solid nanoparticles.
Reduced constituent partial pressures during heating inhibit the formation of locally segregated regions that could nucleate premelting.
Atomic-level near-equimolar homogeneity reduces local compositional fluctuations and minimizes surface segregation of lower-melting components.
CrFeCoNiMo high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can have an atomically homogeneous, near-equimolar elemental distribution.
Suppressing local segregation stabilizes nanoparticle surfaces and bulk structure and delays premelting.
Homogeneous high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will have a higher premelting onset temperature than binary or compositionally segregated nanoparticles.
Homogeneous high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will have a narrower, sharper melting transition than binary or compositionally segregated nanoparticles.
Regions dominated by low-melting elements provoke earlier and more gradual premelting in segregated nanoparticles.
Surface effects are significant for particles approximately 30–100 nm in diameter.
The proposed mixing-entropy control of melting should hold for near-equimolar nanoparticles approximately 30–100 nm in diameter.
Departures from the stated size range or compositional homogeneity may introduce additional melting effects associated with surface defects.
